steps.action: Report from other groups' work that the post-2010 low-level unrest at Sinabung was marked by passive steam plumes and VT earthquakes.
steps.quote: noticed a persistent state of low-level unrest indicated by the occurrence of only passive steam plumes and volcano-tectonic (VT) earthquakes

steps.action: Adopt the published model that VT earthquakes occur on nearby tectonic faults activated by magma migration, as swarms at lateral distances of km to tens of km.
steps.quote: this VT seismicity originates mostly on tectonic fault structures at distances of one or two to tens of kilometers laterally

steps.action: Take the candidate faults mapped by Prambada et al. from surface lineation (mostly strike-slip, one normal fault at Kawar Lake), plus possible hidden faults under deposits.
steps.quote: Prambada et al. 20 estimated the possible faults around the Sinabung area based on surface lineation.

steps.action: State the expectation that activated faults produce lineations of VT clusters from which strike and dip can be estimated.
steps.quote: If they are activated, the clusters of VT events will usually make lineations

steps.action: Report that the earlier magma-migration interpretation of the northern cluster was rejected by GPS studies that found no intrusion-related displacement.
steps.quote: who confirmed that no displacement evidence was related to magma intrusion in this area using GPS observation data

steps.action: Pose the question of which faults the VT events occurred on, using source mechanisms because tomography had not resolved fault structures.
steps.quote: we study the source mechanisms of the VT events of the Sinabung volcano

steps.action: Use three-component 250 Hz seismograms from the six-station CVGHM network deployed to follow the 2010 phreatic eruptions.
steps.quote: three-component seismogram data with 250 Hz sampling rate from the seismometer network (Fig. 1b) deployed by CVGHM from October 2010 to December 2011

steps.action: Take 109 hypocentres (78 double-difference relocated, 31 GAD) and the 1D velocity model from the authors' and co-authors' earlier studies.
steps.quote: The best event locations were obtained by using the DD method (Waldhauser and Ellsworth 26)

steps.action: Adopt Kuge's moment-tensor waveform inversion with Kohketsu reflectivity Green's functions, justified by earlier applications including sparse-network microseismicity.
steps.quote: The focal mechanism inversion method developed by Kuge (13, 14) is applied in this research.

steps.action: Window P-onset-to-S-end waveforms, detrend, taper and filter at 0.2-1.4 Hz in SAC, keeping only 18 of 109 events with usable low-frequency content.
steps.quote: We choose only 18 events from 109 events that can be processed because the filtered waveforms cannot show the proper waveform

steps.action: Invert waveforms for moment tensors and both nodal planes of 18 events, judging the observed-synthetic fit as good (shown for a large and a small event).
steps.quote: The fitting between observational and calculated waveforms is quite good.

steps.action: Group the mechanisms into south-east, normal-faulting and north-west groups and choose one nodal plane per event by similarity and agreement with mapped geology.
steps.quote: We divide all of the beach balls into three groups based on the mechanism similarity and geological consideration.

steps.action: Average the chosen planes of the six south-east events into an oblique sinistral strike-slip fault matching the mapped fault cut by the summit, with dip shown in cross-section.
steps.quote: They are the strike of 44.76°, the dip of 67.83° and the rake of 19.7°.

steps.action: Note that a Mw 5.6 moment-tensor study by another group also indicated this sinistral fault.
steps.quote: The existence of this sinistral fault has been also indicated by Prasetyo et al. 21 from the local event with Mw 5.6.

steps.action: Read pressure axes of the south-east group as pressure from the south, tentatively tied to magma intrusion in the north-east cited from GPS work.
steps.quote: Figure 8 shows that the most possible forces could be pressure from the south

steps.action: Estimate the Kawar Lake normal fault from three normal-faulting events and a curved plane in cross-section, leaving event 10 uninterpreted.
steps.quote: From three events except number 10 in Table 3, the strike, dip and rake are 5.8°, 77.4°, and − 113.2°

steps.action: Propose gravitational collapse as the cause of the normal faulting, with no test.
steps.quote: All these normal faultings could be due [...] .

steps.action: Define a hidden oblique sinistral fault from the hypocentre lineation and averaged mechanisms of the eight north-west events, with pressure axes read as magma pressure from the south.
steps.quote: From their horizontal and vertical distributions, we can define a hidden fault in this area without topography expression.

steps.action: Declare that the hidden-fault result corrects the earlier hypothesis that the north-west cluster reflects magma intrusion.
steps.quote: This result confirms the existence of a hidden fault, which corrects the previous hypothesis that this group relates to magma intrusion.

steps.action: Keep three 'proven' faults (one hidden, two confirmed mapped faults), plotted as the local structure system.
steps.quote: This research revealed one hidden fault that related to the north-west group events and confirmed two possible faults

steps.action: Attribute all events to fault activation by magma-migration stress and set this against similar findings at other volcanoes.
steps.quote: This phenomenon has been also proven by many seismologists

tree.answer: Yes; 18 events fall into three groups whose planes are averaged
Not tested; no sensitivity, synthetic or uncertainty analysis
Three faults declared proven; magma-intrusion hypothesis declared corrected

end.claim: VT events of 2010-2011 at Sinabung occurred on three faults: a hidden oblique sinistral strike-slip fault north-west of the summit (213°/78°/-20°), the mapped oblique strike-slip fault cut by the summit (45°/68°/20°), and the Kawar Lake normal fault (6°/77°/-113°).

decisive_move.sentence: The moment-tensor inversion of 18 VT events and the choice of nodal planes produced the fault parameters; without it neither the hidden fault nor the confirmation of the mapped faults would exist.

gates.evidence: The data come from a network deployed to follow the 2010 eruptions (§1.2 ¶1), not acquired under a hypothesis. The fault claim could have failed if mechanisms were inconsistent or lacked lineation. But nodal planes were chosen partly by 'geological consideration' (§3 ¶2), so agreement with the mapped faults is partly built in. No hypothesis, threshold or grouping criterion is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

novelty_claims.quote: Third, a clear hidden oblique strike-slip was found at the north-west part of the summit.
This research revealed one hidden fault that related to the north-west group events
This result confirms the existence of a hidden fault, which corrects the previous hypothesis that this group relates to magma intrusion.

limits:
Sub-claim statuses:
- Fault strike/dip/rake values: averages with no stated uncertainty or resolution, so short of estimate_with_resolution.
- Stress and magma-pressure readings from P axes: speculative, at most best_explanation.
- Gravitational-collapse origin of the normal faulting: untested hypothesis, status none.

What the paper does not report:
- No synthetic test, alternative velocity model, filter band, station-subset or Green's-function check of the inversion. Fit quality is judged qualitatively ('quite good'), and variance is shown only for the two events in Figs 3-4.
- 91 of 109 events were dropped. Possible selection effects are not discussed.

Possible circularity (inference): nodal planes were chosen using geological consideration, so 'confirming' the mapped faults may partly restate the choice.

The magma-intrusion rival was rejected mainly by cited GPS studies (Hotta et al., Kriswati et al.), not by a test performed here.

Agreement between hypocentre lineation and nodal-plane dip in cross-sections is presented as part of defining the faults, not as an independent check, so it is not coded as V. Fig. 6's caption names only the south-east group, while the text also uses it for the north-west group.

Process not shown (inference from the author-contributions statement): a preliminary set of mechanisms, later improved with relocated hypocentres, is mentioned but not described. The acknowledgements mention reviewer corrections, but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

disagreements.target: The earlier hypothesis that the north-west VT cluster relates to magma migration/intrusion
disagreements.support: Focal mechanisms and hypocentre lineation of eight events define a hidden strike-slip fault; the rejection leans on GPS studies by Hotta et al. and Kriswati et al.
disagreements.quote: This result confirms the existence of a hidden fault, which corrects the previous hypothesis that this group relates to magma intrusion.

disagreements.support: The authors note that the tomography did not resolve fault structures and use source mechanisms instead; no direct comparison is made.
disagreements.quote: Unfortunately, the tomographic results did not resolve the fault structures around the Sinabung area.
